compare.setUp: A 2 kg box pushed by 20 N from rest, for 10 s. Time step dt:
compare.errorAxis: how far off the true position (m)
compare.result: In 10 s the box moves 500 m. With dt = {dt} s, semi-implicit Euler puts it {err} m too far; Velocity Verlet is off by {off}, which is only rounding. Halve dt and Euler's error halves; Verlet stays exact.
compare.why: Both methods get the speed exactly right. Euler uses the speed from the end of each step for the whole step, so it moves the box a little too far every time, and its error grows by ½·a·dt every second. Verlet adds the missing ½·a·dt² and lands on the true position.
compare.intro: The first Octave prototypes used semi-implicit Euler; the simulations now use Velocity Verlet. The test is the one from the Octave prototypes: a constant force, the exact answer worked out by hand, and both methods measured against it.

learn.method1: The simulation does not know the answer in advance. It moves time forward in small, equal steps, called the time step, and at every step it works out where each box goes next from the forces on it. Because the steps are always the same size, the same settings give the same result every time, on any computer.
